sections.h2: Where is Kuna and how fast has it grown?
sections.html:
Kuna is a city in Ada County, part of the Boise metropolitan area, with its business center about 18 miles southwest of downtown Boise. The Census Bureau estimates 31,525 residents as of July 1, 2025.

Growth is the defining fact. The city nearly tripled between 2000 and 2010 and added nearly 60 percent more between 2010 and 2020, which makes it one of the fastest-growing places in Idaho.

The 2020 census found 7,736 households, with 48.2% including children under 18, and a median age of 30.9. There were 7,948 housing units, and the homeowner vacancy rate was 0.8%. For a seller, that is a young, family-heavy market with a lot of newer construction around older farm lots.

sections.h2: What is the history of Kuna?
sections.html:
Kuna began as a railroad stop with coach transport to Boise. The name is popularly said to mean "the end of the trail," although one early account traces it to a Shoshone word meaning "green leaf, good to smoke."

Farming and irrigation shaped the land. Indian Creek, a small seasonal creek, runs through the city and now works as an irrigation canal filled by the New York Canal from the Boise River Diversion Dam. Because canals and ditches run through the area, a buyer's inspector may ask about irrigation rights, ditch easements and drainage on your lot.

South of town are the Kuna Caves, a lava tube, and the Morley Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey National Conservation Area, which holds North America's densest population of nesting raptors. The city calls itself the Gateway to the Birds of Prey, and the Birds of Prey Festival runs each year in mid-May. Kuna Days takes place the first weekend in August.

sections.h2: Why do so many Kuna houses come from new construction?
sections.html:
Kuna's growth is driven by new subdivisions replacing farms and ranches, and that shapes the resale market. The Kuna School District describes a community once made up mostly of farms, ranches and agriculture-based businesses that is now welcoming new residential developments.

The district serves the city, areas of southern Ada County and a small portion of eastern Canyon County, and it reports more than 5,700 students. It expects the student population to grow significantly over the next 10 years based on developments already approved by counties and the city.

A few rules affect what comes next:

  • Idaho does not allow school districts to require impact fees on developments.
  • In July 2022 the Kuna school board approved a voluntary contribution request of about $3,200 per housing unit, which developers may or may not pay.
  • School building bonds in Idaho need a 66 and two-thirds percent supermajority to pass.

For a seller, this means a steady flow of new homes competing with your listing. A resale house in a neighborhood with active builders has to stand out on price and condition.

sections.h2: Who approves permits and development in Kuna?
sections.html:
The City of Kuna handles building permits and planning through its Development Services group. The Building Department conducts plan reviews and monitors by inspection all phases of construction and modifications, and the Planning and Zoning Department is at 751 W. 4th Street, phone (208) 629-8853.

Development decisions run through two bodies. Many projects are reviewed first by the Planning and Zoning Commission, which meets the second and fourth Tuesdays of the month. The City Council meets the first and third Tuesdays and has the final say on developments in the city.

If you finished a garage conversion, deck, shed or basement without a permit, a buyer's agent or lender may ask about it. Check with the Building Department before listing so that an unpermitted item does not appear for the first time in a buyer's inspection report.

Part of Meridian lies inside the Kuna Joint School District 3, so address boundaries can matter when a buyer asks which city or school district applies.

sections.h2: How are property taxes billed and due in Kuna?
sections.html:
Ada County bills property tax for Kuna, and the main bill is due December 20 with an option to pay in two halves. If the first half is paid on time, the second half is due June 20.

Ada County uses three tax rolls, which matters in a fast-building city like Kuna:

RollCoversBill sentDue
Primary (first half or full)Property assessed January 1 to the fourth Monday in MayNovemberDecember 20
Primary (second half)Second installment of the primary billNovemberJune 20
SubsequentProperty assessed fourth Monday in May to October 31JanuaryJune 20
MissedProperty assessed November 1 to December 31FebruaryJune 20

The county explains that extra bills can arrive if you occupied a newly constructed home or made improvements. Sellers of newer Kuna houses should ask the title company whether a subsequent or missed roll bill is still open, because it can come after the primary bill.

Assessment notices go out the first Monday in June, and the last day to appeal a value is the fourth Monday in June. The Idaho State Tax Commission describes the next steps: speak with the assessor, file with the Board of Equalization, then appeal within 30 days to the State Board of Tax Appeals or district court. The homeowner's exemption covers 50% of value, up to $125,000, for an owner-occupied primary home and up to one acre, and it ends when ownership changes. For questions, the Ada County Treasurer lists taxinfo@adacounty.id.gov and 208-287-6800.

sections.h2: What must a Kuna seller disclose under Idaho law?
sections.html:
Idaho Code 55-2504 requires a person transferring one to four unit residential property to complete a property condition disclosure form. That covers sales, exchanges, installment contracts and options, and it applies to nonowner-occupied rentals too.

Section 55-2505 exempts several transfers. These include transfers by a fiduciary in administering an estate, foreclosure transfers, transfers to a spouse or lineal relative, and transfers of newly built homes that were never lived in, although those sellers must still declare annexation and city service status. If you are unsure whether you qualify, ask a licensed Idaho attorney or title officer.

Because many Kuna homes are recent builds, common disclosure topics are drainage, irrigation, and the status of city services. Having those answers ready speeds up any sale route.

sections.h2: What does the 2020 census say about Kuna households and housing?
sections.html:
The 2020 census describes Kuna as a family-oriented, owner-heavy city, and the numbers explain who is likely to buy a Kuna house.

A homeowner vacancy rate under one percent in 2020 pointed to very little unsold inventory at that point. Conditions change, so check recent local sales with a licensed agent before you set a price.

A median household income of $68,017 and a median age of 30.9 point to a buyer pool that includes young families. Buyers who finance may ask for repairs or credits, while a cash buyer does not need loan approval.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work for a Kuna house?
sections.html:
In a direct cash sale the buyer does not need a lender, so the schedule depends on your readiness and on title work. You request an offer, the buyer reviews the property, and a title company handles closing and pays off any mortgage or taxes from your proceeds.

  • List what you know: occupancy, liens, back taxes, HOA status and repairs.
  • Compare the offer with listing costs, repair estimates and carrying costs such as utilities and taxes.
  • Pick a closing date that fits your move.

This route tends to fit owners facing relocation, an inherited house, a tenant problem or repairs they cannot fund. You owe nothing if you decline an offer, and a local agent can give a second opinion on a listing.

faqs.q: How many people live in Kuna?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau estimates 31,525 residents as of July 1, 2025. The 2020 census counted 24,011 and the 2010 census counted 15,210.

faqs.q: Which county collects property tax in Kuna?
faqs.a: Ada County does. The first half or full payment is due December 20, and the second half is due June 20 if the first half was paid on time.

faqs.q: Can I get an extra tax bill after selling a newer Kuna home?
faqs.a: It is possible. Ada County issues subsequent and missed roll bills in January and February for improvements or occupancy assessed after the primary roll, both due June 20, so ask your title company to check.

faqs.q: Does Kuna charge school impact fees on new homes?
faqs.a: No. Idaho does not allow school districts to require impact fees. The Kuna School District asks developers for a voluntary contribution of about $3,200 per housing unit.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit record to sell my Kuna house?
faqs.a: Not as a separate requirement, but buyers often ask about permits for additions and conversions. The City of Kuna Building Department can tell you what is on file.

faqs.q: Is a disclosure form required for a Kuna sale?
faqs.a: Usually. Idaho Code 55-2504 requires one for one to four unit residential property, with exemptions in 55-2505 such as estate and foreclosure transfers.
